item.title: Drought Surcharge on Your Water Bill: What It Is and Why You
item.description:
Quick Answer

**A drought surcharge** is an extra fee water utilities add during dry periods to discourage high usage and cover increased supply costs. The fee is **tiered based on usage**—the more water you consume, especially outdoors, the higher the charge.

  • Drought surcharges add **$7-$76 per month** to your bill depending on usage tier
  • Example: Denver Water charges **$1.10 per 1,000 gallons** in Tier 2 and **$2.20 per 1,000 gallons** in Tier 3

Track your [monthly water usage](/blog/05-how-to-lower-utility-bills) to stay in lower tiers and reduce costs.

item.title: Tiered Water Rates Explained: Why Using More Costs Dramatically More
item.description:
Quick Answer

**Tiered water rates** charge higher prices per gallon as you use more water. Instead of a flat rate, usage is divided into blocks—essential indoor needs get lower rates while outdoor/excessive use gets charged higher rates.

  • Example: First **10,000 gallons** might cost **$4.00 per 1,000 gallons**, but usage above **20,000 gallons** can cost **$10.00 per 1,000 gallons**
  • Impact: Using **25,000 gallons** could cost **$150**, while using **15,000 gallons** only costs **$70**—more than double the cost for **66% less water**

Check your [water bill tier thresholds](/blog/02-average-utility-costs-2026) to avoid crossing into expensive pricing blocks.

item.title: Average Water Usage Per Person: A Practical Range
item.description:
Quick Answer

The average person uses 80-100 gallons of water per day, with indoor use averaging 60-70 gallons (70% of total) and outdoor use making up the remaining 30%. Toilet flushing (24 gallons), showers (20 gallons), and faucet use (15 gallons) account for the largest indoor shares, while lawn irrigation can add 30-100+ gallons daily in warmer months.

  • Toilet = 24 gallons/day (30%) - Old toilets use 3.5-5 gallons per flush vs. 1.28 gallons for efficient models
  • Showers = 20 gallons/day (25%) - Low-flow showerheads save 7,500 gallons/year per person
  • Faucets = 15 gallons/day (19%) - Fixing leaks saves 10% on water bills ($50-100/year)

See how to budget for utilities for cost management.

item.title: Water Service Charge Explained: What the Fixed Fee Covers (and Why You Still Pay It)
item.description:
The problem: your bill has a charge even when you used almost no water

You did not water the lawn. You were out of town. The usage on your bill looks tiny. And yet there it is: a water "service charge," "base charge," "customer charge," or "meter charge."

That moment is frustrating because it feels like you are paying for nothing.

You are not paying for "nothing," but you also should not have to guess what the fee means. This guide explains it in plain English and shows you how to sanity-check what you are being charged.

item.title: Why Did My Water Bill Suddenly Increase?
item.description:
Quick Answer

A sudden water bill increase usually indicates a leak (toilet, pipe, or irrigation), rate changes, or seasonal usage spikes.

  • A running toilet wastes 200–300 gallons/day** — adds $50**–$150/month
  • Hidden leaks account for 10,000+ gallons/month** before detection
  • Seasonal rates increase 10–20% in summer due to peak demand

[For more detail, see common causes of high utility bills.]

The most common reasons for a sudden spike

Sudden increases are usually tied to leaks, seasonal outdoor use, or a change in household habits. Toilets are a frequent cause because a silent leak can run all day without being obvious. A running toilet can waste hundreds of gallons per day.

item.title: Why Is My Water Bill Higher in Summer? (7 Common Causes + What to Check First)
item.description:
The problem: summer arrives and your bill suddenly feels out of control

Summer water bills have a pattern: they look normal, then the heat arrives, and the next statement is noticeably higher.

The tricky part is that "summer" is not one cause. It is a mix of outdoor use, faster evaporation, and sometimes rate structures that get more expensive as usage rises.

This guide helps you identify what changed in your case so you can stop guessing and start checking the right things.

item.title: How to Read a Water Meter (and Know If Its Accurate)
item.description:
Quick Answer

Water meters measure in cubic feet or gallons: Read the first 4-5 numbers (black on white) to get your usage, then subtract the previous reading. Most residential usage is 80-150 gallons per person daily ($40-80/month typical).

  • Fact: A running toilet can waste 200-400 gallons daily, adding $50-100 to monthly bills
  • Action: Check your meter while all water is off - if it’s still moving, you have a leak

For more detail, see Understanding Utility Bills.

item.title: What Is CCF on a Water Bill? (Cubic Feet Explained in Plain English)
item.description:
Quick Answer

CCF means "hundred cubic feet" — 1 CCF equals 748 gallons of water. A typical household uses about 2–4 CCF per person per month; if your number is well above that range, a hidden leak (most often a running toilet) is the usual reason. CCF is just the volume unit your bill uses — the fee comes from the rate your utility charges per CCF.
